summary: On 8 July 2022 Rogers's network in Canada failed after a routing filter was deleted in its core networks, which overwhelmed router capacity. Millions of customers lost service and 911 was affected. Rogers committed to separating wireless and wireline traffic and more testing.

overview.background: Rogers runs wireless and wireline services over a shared core. Routers decide how traffic flows. The page was Rogers' CTO account as reported by ITWorldCanada.
systems: Core network routers from more than one vendor
A routing filter on distribution routers
Wireless and wireline services on a shared core
overview.impact: Millions of Canadians lost connectivity and 911 services were affected across the country.
overview.severity: A national outage. The article does not give the duration; the card says about a day.
overview.gaps: The article does not state the year. The case card gives 2022. This file uses that.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: A deleted filter overwhelms router capacity
diagrams.caption: Per Rogers, deleting a routing filter overwhelmed router capacity, and the update behaved differently on hardware from different vendors.

diagrams.title: Separated networks and failover (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Rogers said it would separate wireless and wireline traffic and add failover to a competitor's network. This picture shows the idea.

nodes.label: Failover to another network within seconds

afterChanges: A fault on one side does not take down the other.
Emergency calls have a second path.
Changes are tested on every vendor.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: A routing filter is deleted in the core networks during an update.
Routers are overwhelmed and the network stops carrying traffic.
Wireless, internet and 911 services are affected for millions.
Rogers finds the update behaved differently across vendors.
Rogers commits to separating wireless and wireline traffic (about C$250 million).
Service returns and Rogers names Ron McKenzie as CTO replacing Jorge Fernandes.

rootCause.trigger: A routing filter was deleted in the core during an update.
rootCause.underlying: The update was handled differently by hardware from different vendors, which Rogers had not anticipated, and the error got past testing.
contributing: Wireless and wireline shared a core
Management dependence on the same core (per the case card, not the article)

evidence.label: Vendor behaviour
evidence.note: McKenzie's description of behaviour between vendors, as quoted by ITWorldCanada.

evidence.label: A simulated pre-change check
evidence.body:
show route summary | match 'routes'
show bgp neighbor | match prefixes
evidence.note: Generic checks of route counts before and after a filter change. Not Rogers commands.

diagnose.step: Compare routing table sizes before and after.
Check whether management traffic uses the same core.

fix.safety: Never remove a filter in production without a dry run on every router type.

troubleshoot.scenario: A network change removed a filter and the core is down. Multiple vendors' routers run in the core.
clues: Management tools use the same network
troubleshoot.question: How do you recover and prevent a repeat?
hints: How do you protect emergency calls?
troubleshoot.answer: Restore the filter, recover in stages, test on every vendor, separate networks and add a failover for emergency calls.

remediation.answer: Run the change in a lab with each router type.

design.prompt: Design a carrier core where one change cannot take down everything.
design.answer: Separate domains, staged changes, multi-vendor testing, failover and out-of-band management.

checks.q: Did the article give the duration?

options: Different vendors' hardware handled the update differently
